content: The Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) AIDS hypothesis suggests that the AIDS pandemic originated from live polio vaccines prepared in chimpanzee tissue cultures, which were likely contaminated with Simian Immunodeficiency Virus (SIV) from chimpanzees. These vaccines were administered to approximately one million Africans between 1957 and 1960. The populations who received these vaccines, potentially without being fully informed of the risks, were among the first in the world to experience HIV-1 infections and AIDS approximately five years later. Specifically, the experimental oral vaccine known as CHAT-1 is alleged to have been contaminated with SIV, a group of viruses endemic to African primates and widely accepted as the origin of HIV. Evidence suggests that CHAT-1 may have been amplified in African facilities using tissue cultures derived from chimpanzee kidneys and serum, which contained macrophages, the primary target of immunodeficiency viruses. The OPV AIDS hypothesis has been widely discredited by the scientific community, as it is contradicted by substantial scientific evidence. Two vaccines are used globally to combat polio: the inactivated polio vaccine (IPV), developed by Jonas Salk, and the oral polio vaccine (OPV), a live-attenuated vaccine. IPV is made from three wild, virulent strains of poliovirus grown in monkey kidney tissue cultures and inactivated with formalin. OPV, on the other hand, is produced by passing the virus through non-human cells at sub-physiological temperatures, inducing mutations that reduce its ability to infect nervous tissue. Both vaccines have been used for decades to induce immunity to polio and prevent the spread of the infection. OPV has advantages such as ease of administration, low cost, and suitability for mass vaccination campaigns. It also mimics natural infection by targeting the gastrointestinal tract, the primary site of poliovirus replication, and provides long-lasting immunity. The CHAT vaccine, an oral polio vaccine developed by Hilary Koprowski, was one of several attenuated vaccine strains created in the 1950s. Koprowski's CHAT strain was administered to approximately one million people in the Belgian Congo (now the Democratic Republic of the Congo), Rwanda, and Burundi between 1957 and 1960. During this period, it was common practice to amplify vaccines locally using tissue cultures from native animals. In Africa, for example, African green monkey tissue was used to amplify the Sabin vaccine, while baboons were used in French West Africa. In Poland, the CHAT vaccine was amplified using Asian macaques. In 2003, Edward Hooper and colleagues traveled to the Democratic Republic of the Congo and claimed to uncover testimony supporting the OPV AIDS hypothesis. They alleged that batches of the CHAT vaccine had been prepared locally using tissue cultures from chimpanzees at the Lindi Camp, a chimpanzee colony near the Laboratoire Médical de Stanleyville (LMS). However, these claims were disputed by Paul Osterrieth, who was in charge of the virology department at LMS. Osterrieth stated that no vaccines were prepared locally and that only the CHAT vaccine from America was used. The OPV AIDS hypothesis was first proposed by San Antonio physician Eva Lee Snead, who incorrectly suggested that SV40 might be a precursor to HIV. In 1987, Louis Pascal independently concluded that Koprowski's CHAT vaccine, administered in the Belgian Congo between 1957 and 1960, was a likely source of HIV. Pascal's paper on the theory was rejected by multiple scientific journals. Journalist Edward Hooper later became convinced of the hypothesis and detailed it in his 1999 book, The River. A 2004 television documentary, The Origin of AIDS, strongly supported the OPV hypothesis. For over 15 years, the OPV AIDS hypothesis has been criticized by the scientific and medical community as unfounded and inconsistent with HIV epidemiology. In 1992, an independent panel found the hypothesis problematic at every proposed step. In 2001, multiple studies published in Nature and Science strongly argued against any link between the polio vaccine and AIDS. A 2004 study in Nature further demonstrated that while SIV was present in chimpanzees in the Kisangani area, the strain of SIV infecting these chimpanzees was phylogenetically distinct from all strains of HIV, providing direct evidence that these chimpanzees were not the source of HIV in humans.
